### Policy writing

**Response to the Danish Ministry of Finance on the price effects of a food VAT reduction**,
August 2026. The Ministry's reply to Question No. 16 of the Folketing Finance Committee cited
our 2020 study and set it aside as an average across goods. This memo re-estimates the result
for food alone and for the kind of rate change Denmark is proposing, and reviews the evidence
the Ministry assembled.

### Where the research is used

The VAT pass-through results are used in the technical literature of the IMF, the World Bank,
the OECD, the European Commission's Joint Research Centre, the Bank of Greece and the Banco de
España, and in government and parliamentary analysis in Japan and Austria.

A [Japanese Cabinet Secretariat working
group](https://www.cas.go.jp/jp/seisaku/kokuminkaigi/contents/20260424/minutes.pdf) considering
the 2027 food consumption-tax cut recorded average pass-through of 13 percent on VAT reductions
against 55 percent on increases, across all EU VAT changes between 1996 and 2015, alongside the
Argentine evidence that prices settled above their pre-cut level once the tax was restored
except where increases were regulated. The [Austrian Parliament's
Budgetdienst](https://www.parlament.gv.at/fachinfos/budgetdienst/Senkung-der-Umsatzsteuer-auf-ausgewaehlte-Nahrungsmittel)
used the same asymmetry in its May 2026 analysis of the food-VAT cut.

Selected citations: IMF Working Paper 25/165, *Efficiency Aspects of the VAT*; World Bank Policy
Research Working Paper 10677, *VAT Rate Structures in Theory and Practice*; OECD Taxation Working
Paper 49, *Reassessing the Regressivity of the VAT*; European Commission Joint Research Centre,
*Price Effects of Temporary VAT Rate Cuts: Evidence from Spanish Supermarkets*.
